objective: Unwrapping the Rings. Now comes the key trick: cut each ring and lay it flat. A thin ring becomes a thin rectangle! Its width equals the circumference at that radius (2πr), and its height equals the ring's thickness. Adjust the number of rings to see how the approximation improves

finalists.title: Rectangle Width Error Correction Interface
finalists.narrative_wrapper: The student sees one unwrapped ring displayed as a rectangle with visible width and thickness. A measurement error indicator shows how much the rectangle's width deviates from the 'ideal' circumference for that ring's radius. The student drags this error bar to zero or to specific error targets, and the system inversely adjusts which ring is shown and how the circle is segmented.
finalists.manipulated_variable: The measurement error between the displayed rectangle's width and the theoretical circumference 2πr for its radius, which inversely determines which ring index is displayed and how finely the circle is subdivided
finalists.primary_visual_feedback: As the student drags the error indicator toward zero, the circle view highlights different rings in sequence and may re-subdivide itself into more or fewer total rings, while the rectangle width and thickness values update, and the highlighted ring on the circle pulses to show correspondence
finalists.goal_structure: Commit-a-prediction-then-reveal: student predicts which ring number (innermost=1, outermost=N) will have a specific error value, commits the prediction, then manipulates the error slider to that value to see if the predicted ring appears highlighted
finalists.causal_chain_exposed: Live annotations show: (1) the current ring's radius r, (2) the calculated ideal circumference 2πr, (3) the actual displayed rectangle width, (4) the error magnitude and sign, and (5) the total number of rings and current ring index, making the quantization effect of discrete rings visible
finalists.trace_strategy: Each time the student achieves zero error for a ring, a small checkmark appears at that ring's position on the circle, building up a visual record of which rings have been 'calibrated' and revealing patterns about inner vs. outer ring errors
finalists.aha_moment: Discovering that error cannot be eliminated for all rings simultaneously unless the number of rings approaches infinity, and that individual ring errors become arbitrarily small as subdivision increases—connecting discrete approximation to continuous limit
finalists.feasibility_sketch: Requires custom SVG/canvas code for dynamic ring subdivision and error visualization, but feasible within a web page.
finalists.weakness: The complexity of the interaction might overwhelm students without sufficient scaffolding or prior knowledge.

finalists.title: Ring Unwrapping Slider with Side-by-Side Views
finalists.narrative_wrapper: Students see a circle divided into rings on the left. They adjust a slider to control how many rings the circle is divided into. As they change the number, they watch each ring get cut and unfold into rectangles on the right side, stacked vertically.
finalists.manipulated_variable: A slider control that changes the number of rings the circle is divided into (from perhaps 3 to 50 rings)
finalists.primary_visual_feedback: The circle re-divides into more or fewer concentric rings, and simultaneously the stack of rectangles on the right updates to show correspondingly thinner or thicker rectangles, maintaining visual correspondence through color or animation
finalists.goal_structure: Free exploration with implicit guidance toward increasing ring count to observe rectangles becoming more uniform in width
finalists.causal_chain_exposed: Each ring displays its radius value r, the corresponding rectangle shows its width labeled as 2πr, and its height labeled as dr or Δr; total area of rectangles displayed numerically approaching πr²
finalists.trace_strategy: None - the current state is sufficient because the concept focuses on the geometric transformation at the current subdivision level, not the progression over time
finalists.aha_moment: Discovering that as rings get thinner (higher ring count), the rectangles become nearly identical in width, revealing they can be rearranged into a parallelogram or triangle shape with base πr and height r
finalists.feasibility_sketch: The design requires a slider, SVG/canvas for drawing rings and rectangles, and live readouts for dimensions; all standard web UI components.
finalists.weakness: The design may not explicitly guide learners to the aha moment without additional narrative cues.

narrative_draft.text:
We've sliced our circle into thin rings, but rings don't make it easy to see where πr² comes from. Here's the breakthrough: imagine taking scissors to one of those rings, snipping it open, and laying it flat on the table. What you get is nearly a rectangle. The width of that rectangle is the circumference at that radius—2πr—and its height is just the thickness of the ring.

But there's a problem hiding in the word "nearly." Try adjusting the error indicator to bring the rectangle width exactly to the theoretical circumference 2πr for different rings. You'll notice something strange: you can get one ring perfect, but when you switch to a different ring, the error creeps back in. The inner rings want to curve more tightly than the outer ones, so they resist being flattened into true rectangles. Push the error toward zero and watch which ring the system highlights—when you demand less error, you're forced to look at thinner and thinner rings from a more finely divided circle.

This is the heart of why calculus works. We can't make every ring a perfect rectangle unless we use infinitely many rings, each infinitely thin. But as you subdivide more and more, the error for any individual ring shrinks toward zero. When we write πr² as the area formula, we're really saying "the limit of all these imperfect rectangles as they become perfect."
